title: The Fort Built on a Human Sacrifice Is Still Paying Off the Debt
standfirst: Rao Jodha founded Mehrangarh in 1459 after a hermit's curse and a volunteer buried alive in its foundations, a bargain his family still honours. What followed was a twenty-eight-year war for the fort, funerals that cost dozens of women's lives, and, by 1971, a Maharaja selling bat guano to pay the bills.

sections.heading: A Hermit's Curse Got Answered With a Man Buried Alive in the Foundations
sections.body:
Rao Jodha broke ground on 12 May 1459, moving his capital nine kilometres south from Mandore to a rock outcrop then called Bhakurcheeria — the mountain of birds. Its only occupant was a hermit, Cheeria Nathji, "the lord of birds," who did not want to leave. He went, in the end, but not quietly: Jodha was [cursed with the words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehrangarh) "Jodha! May your citadel ever suffer a scarcity of water!"

Appeasing the hermit with a house and a temple inside the new walls wasn't enough on its own. To guarantee the site would hold, the builders turned to something more literal than architecture: a man of the Meghwal caste, Raja Ram Meghwal, [volunteered to be buried](https://homegrown.co.in/homegrown-voices/blood-on-the-sandstone-unraveling-the-ancient-curse-of-jodhpurs-mehrangar-fort) alive in the foundations, on condition that his family be provided for permanently. A tablet marking the spot still stands just inside the Dedh Kangra Pol, and by one contemporary account his descendants [are still supported](https://thrillingtravel.in/mehrangarh-fort-haunted-story-facts.html) today by a Rathore family trust — a bargain now five and a half centuries old and, as far as the record shows, still being paid.

sections.heading: The Fort Sits on Rock a Geological Survey Now Protects By Law
sections.body:
Mehrangarh rises 122 metres above the plains on an outcrop where two ancient rock formations meet — the Malani Igneous Suite against the Jodhpur Group, laid down during what Wikipedia's own account of the site calls ["the last phase of igneous activity"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehrangarh) of the Precambrian era anywhere on the Indian subcontinent. The Geological Survey of India has since declared the contact point a National Geological Monument, protected in its own right, independently of the fort built on top of it.

What was raised on that rock is startling by any measure: walls up to 36 metres high and 21 metres thick, enclosing a five-kilometre hilltop compound of 486 hectares. Almost none of it dates to Rao Jodha's own lifetime. Most of the fort as it now stands was built more than a century and a half later, during the reign of Maharaja Jaswant Singh, between 1638 and 1678 — the ruler whose death without an heir on record would trigger a war for the fort that lasted almost as long as his reign had.

sections.heading: The Infant Heir Spent Nearly Thirty Years Fighting to Get the Fort Back
sections.body:
Jaswant Singh died in November 1678. His heir, Ajit Singh, was born only after his father's death, straight into a fight for his own throne — the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb had already sent his own son, Prince Akbar, to occupy Jodhpur. Durgadas Rathore, a general who had served the old Maharaja, [disguised the infant's mothers as men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rathore_rebellion_%281679%E2%80%931707%29) to smuggle the baby out of Mughal-held Delhi that same year, then spent close to three decades fighting to put him on the throne for real.

The war reached the fort itself, more than once. Mughal officers held Jodhpur for stretches of the rebellion, and Rajput loyalists are recorded retaking the fort from them before Ajit Singh, by then grown, defeated the Mughal garrison commander and secured the city for good on 12 March 1707 — nine days after Aurangzeb's own death removed any hope of reinforcement. Fateh Pol, the gate still standing at the fort's entrance, was raised that same year to mark it. Twenty-eight years of war, in other words, built into a doorway.

sections.heading: What a Royal Funeral Cost the Women Who Lived There
sections.body:
The fort's ledger of what it cost the people around it runs beyond soldiers. When Ajit Singh — the same man who had spent his infancy in hiding and his adulthood at war to win the place — died in 1731, six wives and fifty-eight concubines [walked onto his funeral pyre](https://www.travelgumbo.com/gumbos-pic-of-the-day-13-dec-2013-sati-handprints-15-jodphur-queens-left-their-handprints/) and were burned with him. More than a century later, when Maharaja Man Singh died in 1843, women of his household are said to have pressed their hands into wet plaster at the Loha Pol gate on their way out to do the same; the gilded marks are still maintained there today.

Wikipedia's own description of the gate is careful to say the handprints span "over the years" and several reigns, not one death — and the wider record backs that caution. Self-immolation persisted among the ruling families of Jodhpur and other Rajput states well into the nineteenth century, [decades after](https://worldhistorycommons.org/sati-handprints) the British government outlawed the practice by law in territory it directly controlled, in 1829.

sections.heading: When the Government Stopped Paying, the Maharaja Sold Bat Droppings to Farmers
sections.body:
The fort's finances stayed a Rathore problem long after India's independence. Gaj Singh II inherited it in 1952, at the age of four, and in the early 1970s the government of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi abolished the privy purse that had paid India's former royal families a fixed annual allowance — for Singh, [$125,000 a year](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/royal-palaces-maharaja-culture-india-180957796/), gone at a stroke. "We became the bad boys," he said of what followed.

He met the shortfall with whatever was at hand, including bat guano scraped from the fort's own chambers and sold as fertiliser to chilli farmers, and converting the family's 347-room Umaid Bhawan Palace into a hotel. The steadier fix came from the fort itself: in 1972 Singh formed the [Mehrangarh Museum Trust](https://www.mehrangarh.org/about-us/) and handed over his own ancestral fortress; the trust registered with the Rajasthan government in 1974, opened the fort to the public that year, and now draws over a million paying visitors annually. The palace Rao Jodha's descendants once ruled from now covers its own costs by being looked at.
